name: When Students May Use AI in Math
title: When Students May Use AI in Math
answer: Math teachers should set clear rules for when students may use AI, just as they already do for calculators. Some assignments build basic skills that must be done by hand, while others focus on problem solving where a tool can handle routine steps. Clear levels help students and families understand the purpose of each task and reduce integrity problems.

sections.body: This idea applies the same kind of rule that math teachers have long used for calculators to the use of AI. Some assignments are meant to build basic skills that students need to do by hand, while others focus on problem solving where a tool can handle routine steps. The AI use levels from Chapter 3 work well here, so a fluency quiz might be marked no AI while a data project might allow AI for organizing and graphing. Clear levels help students and families understand the purpose of each task. The rules remove guessing, which is where most integrity problems start.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, teachers mark each task with a clear AI use level. A parent who sees that tonight's homework is marked no AI knows the child should work alone. A student who sees that a project allows AI for checking work knows how to use the tool honestly. Showing work matters more than ever, because when a student writes out each step the teacher can see the reasoning and spot where it went wrong. Many math teachers now give most of the credit for the process, which also makes it easier to see whether a student understands the method.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or finding for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research, drawing on the long-standing practice of deciding when students may use calculators and on the AI use levels from Chapter 3.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks are that an answer alone could have come from anywhere, so showing work matters more than ever. The decisions about which assignments are no AI and which allow AI stay with the teacher, who must judge the purpose of each task. Students and families need the levels to be clear so they are not left guessing. The teacher also decides how much credit goes to the process rather than the answer.
